chunks: Ali, from Muhammad, from Yunus, from Aban, from Sulayman ibn Harun who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Allah has not created anything permissible nor anything forbidden except that there is a limit for it, like the boundary of a house. Whatever falls on the road side belongs to the road, and whatever falls on the house side belongs to the house — even the compensation for a scratch, and what is beyond it, and the lash, and half a lash.'

key_terms.أَرْشُ الْخَدْشِ: Compensation (arsh) for a scratch — the smallest quantifiable injury in classical Islamic law
key_terms.الْجَلْدَة: The lash — a unit of corporal punishment in Islamic penal law
key_terms.حَدٌّ: Limit, boundary — in fiqh, refers to precisely defined legal thresholds and punishments
key_terms.حَلَال وَحَرَام: Permissible and forbidden — the fundamental dyad of Islamic jurisprudence

ai.seo_question: Does Islamic law have defined limits for every permissible and forbidden act?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) teaches that every divine ruling — whether permissible or forbidden — has precise boundaries, using the metaphor of a house's property line. Just as the line between a house and a public road is definitive and clear, so too are God's limits in law, extending even to the most minor matters such as the blood-money for a scratch or half a lash in punishment. This hadith affirms the comprehensiveness of divine legislation and is cited in chapters on the sufficiency of the Quran and Sunnah as the complete source of law.
